passage:
"You forgot my birthday, Sahil. Even Mummy's cousin in Canada remembered."
Sahil put his phone down. "I'm sorry, Lavu. I got caught up with the match."
"You always get caught up."
He opened his mouth to defend himself, then stopped. "You're right. I keep saying sorry and then doing it again."
Lavanya crossed her arms. "So?"
"So I've been thinking about what kind of brother I want to be. Not the one who remembers because Mummy reminds him."
"Then what kind?"
"The kind you can count on. When you have exams, I'll do your chores. And I'm putting your birthday in my calendar for the next ten years."
Lavanya almost smiled. "Eleven."

qa.q: Why did Sahil say he forgot the birthday?
qa.a: He got caught up with the match.

qa.q: Why did Sahil stop himself from defending himself?
qa.a: He felt sorry, realising Lavanya was right about his pattern, and wanted to own it instead of making excuses.

qa.q: What makes Sahil's promise more believable than a plain sorry?
qa.a: He named specific actions, like doing her chores during exams and putting the date in his calendar.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's "Eleven" suggest about how she sees him now?
qa.a: She is softening and willing to give him a chance, teasing him as a sign the hurt is easing. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teenager deciding what kind of brother he wants to be after letting his sister down.

passage: Last winter Sangeeta told me her parents were fighting a lot and she was sleeping at her aunt's. Two other people in our group asked, "Lalit, what's going on with her?" and I realised I had a choice. I could be the guy who knows things and passes them on, which, honestly, I used to be. Or I could be something else. I told them, "Ask her if you want to know." Then I just kept showing up. Walking her to the bus. Not asking too much. I think that's when I figured out what kind of friend I want to be: the one people can tell things to without it going anywhere. It changed how I see myself, not just her.

qa.q: Where was Sangeeta sleeping?
qa.a: At her aunt's.

qa.q: What choice did Lalit feel he faced when others asked about Sangeeta?
qa.a: Lalit felt torn between staying the guy who passes things on and becoming a friend who keeps things private.

qa.q: What could Lalit also do if Sangeeta seemed very low for a long time?
qa.a: Gently encourage her to talk to a trusted adult or the school counsellor, while still being there as a friend.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta experience Lalit "just showing up"?
qa.a: As steady, quiet support that doesn't make her explain or relive things. 🤍

grounding: It shows a teenager choosing the kind of friend he wants to be when a friend confides in him.

passage: School counsellor's note, Aparna. Reena, fifteen, came to talk again today. She said she has always been "the easy friend": agreeing to every plan, lending notes, never saying no. Last week she lent her project file and got it back torn, and she said nothing. Today she said, "I want to be a good friend, but I don't want to disappear." We talked about what she values: loyalty, honesty, fun. She wrote a line on a sticky note: "Kind, not a doormat." She plans to tell her friend about the file, calmly. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What happened to the project file Reena lent?
qa.a: It came back torn.

qa.q: What did Reena mean by "I don't want to disappear"?
qa.a: She was worried that always agreeing was making her lose herself, and she wanted her own needs to count in friendships too.

qa.q: Why is telling her friend about the file calmly a good first step?
qa.a: It lets Reena practise speaking up in a small, specific situation without ending the friendship.

qa.q: How might Reena's friend react when Reena mentions the file?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since Reena never complained before, but it could also make the friendship more honest.

grounding: It shows, in a counsellor's note, a teenager deciding what kind of friend she wants to be.

passage: Tuesday night. Something small happened today but I can't stop thinking. At lunch the girls were laughing about Dilnaz's new haircut and I laughed too, and even added a joke. Then Dilnaz walked in and sat next to me like normal, and I felt sick. She has been my friend since Class 3. When Ammi was in hospital last year, Dilnaz came every evening with my notes. And I sold her out for one laugh. I don't want to be like that. I want to be the one who says 'leave it' even if it's awkward. Tomorrow I'll tell her, maybe not everything, but that I was mean and I'm sorry. And next time I'll actually say 'leave it' out loud. – Parveen

qa.q: Since which class has Dilnaz been Parveen's friend?
qa.a: Since Class 3.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel sick when Dilnaz sat next to her?
qa.a: Parveen felt guilty for having just joked about a friend who had always been loyal.

qa.q: What would you advise Parveen for tomorrow?
qa.a: Apologise simply and honestly, then show the change by speaking up the next time the group mocks someone.

qa.q: If you were Dilnaz, what would you want from Parveen?
qa.a: I would want an honest apology and to know Parveen will stand by me when I'm not in the room. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend she wants to be after letting a loyal friend down.

passage:
Hansa: i yelled at chotu again today. he just wanted me to see his drawing
Mahima: u were studying na?
Hansa: yes but i didn't even look up. he walked off so quietly 😔
Mahima: ugh that quiet walk away is the worst
Hansa: i keep saying i want to be the didi YOU were to me
Hansa: you always had 5 min for me even in your boards year
Mahima: haha i also yelled plenty, trust me
Mahima: but ya, 5 min is doable
Hansa: ok new rule. when he comes, pen down for 5 min. timer if needed
Mahima: and say sorry for today
Hansa: already did. he showed me the drawing. it's a dinosaur with my face 😅
Mahima: perfect. frame it ❤️

qa.q: What did Hansa's little brother want her to do?
qa.a: He wanted her to see his drawing.

qa.q: What does Hansa's sad emoji after 'he walked off so quietly' reveal?
qa.a: It shows she felt guilty and hurt seeing how quietly he gave up on her.

qa.q: What makes Hansa's new rule a good step?
qa.a: It is small and concrete, five minutes with the pen down, so she can keep it even while studying.

qa.q: How might Hansa's little brother experience the change?
qa.a: He would feel noticed and important when she stops for him, instead of learning not to ask.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing what kind of older sister she wants to be, modelled on her cousin.
